lead: A machine part must pass two different tests. Strength asks whether it can carry its loads without yielding or breaking: the largest stress must stay below the allowable stress. Stiffness asks whether it deforms too much to do its job: the deflection or angle of twist must stay below a limit set by the machine, such as gear alignment or the accuracy of a cutting tool. Both tests use the same loads and the same trial section but different section properties, and the larger of the two sizes is the answer. Long shafts, slender beams and precision frames are usually sized by stiffness.
prereq: You need factor of safety and the stress formulas.

blocks.text: Strength: σmax ≤ σallow = Syt/n; stiffness: δmax ≤ δallow, θ ≤ θallow

σ<sub>max</sub> is the largest working stress (MPa) and n the factor of safety; δ<sub>max</sub> is the largest deflection (mm) and θ the angle of twist (rad or degrees); the limits come from the function of the machine or from a design guide.

Bending strength depends on the section modulus Z = I/c, bending stiffness on the second moment I. Torsional strength depends on J/r, torsional stiffness on J. Stiffness also depends on the material through E or G, while strength depends on S<sub>yt</sub>. Since every steel has about the same E (200 GPa) and G (80 GPa), a stronger steel does nothing for a stiffness-limited part; only a larger section does.

δ is the extension of a bar of length L (mm) and area A (mm²) under an axial load P (N); θ is the angle of twist (rad) of a shaft of length L under torque T (N·mm); E and G are the moduli of elasticity and rigidity (N/mm²); J is the polar second moment of area (mm⁴). Multiply θ in rad by 180/π for degrees.

head: Beam and load
Largest deflection
rows: Cantilever, uniform load w over its length

blocks.text: In the table, P is a point load (N), w a load per unit length (N/mm), L the span (mm), E the modulus of elasticity (N/mm²) and I the second moment of area of the section about the bending axis (mm⁴). Bending deflection grows with L³ and torsional twist only with L, which is why slender beams are almost always stiffness-limited, and long shafts are when a twist limit is set. A common limit for transmission shafts is 0.25° of twist per metre of length.

sections.h3: The design loop: trial, strength, stiffness, resize

items: Choose the material and the allowable stress S<sub>yt</sub>/n.
Express the section by one unknown (diameter d, or width b with depth h = 2b).
Size for strength: set σ<sub>max</sub> = σ<sub>allow</sub> and solve for the unknown.
Size for stiffness: set δ or θ equal to its limit and solve again.
Take the larger size, round it up to a standard (preferred) size, and recheck both stress and deflection at that size.

blocks.text: Figure 1.8.1 plots both requirements for the beam of the first worked example. Strength wins for short, heavily loaded parts; stiffness wins for long, lightly loaded ones; the final part must pass both.

examples.question: A simply supported steel beam of span 1.2 m carries a central load of 10 kN. The allowable bending stress is 120 MPa, the allowable deflection 3 mm and E = 200 GPa. The section is rectangular with depth h = 2b. Find the smallest width b and the deflection at the chosen size.
steps: Data: P = 10,000 N; L = 1200 mm; σ<sub>allow</sub> = 120 MPa; δ<sub>allow</sub> = 3 mm; E = 200,000 N/mm².
Section: I = b(2b)³/12 = (2/3)b⁴; Z = I/(h/2) = I/b = (2/3)b³.
Strength needs the larger width. Round up to b = 34 mm, h = 68 mm.
examples.answer: Strength governs: b ≥ 33.47 mm against 30.80 mm for stiffness. Use 34 mm × 68 mm, with σ = 114.5 MPa and δ = 2.02 mm.

examples.question: A solid steel shaft transmits 10 kW at 240 rpm. The allowable shear stress is 40 MPa, the twist must not exceed 0.25° per metre, and G = 80 GPa. Find the diameter.
steps: Stiffness governs. Take the standard size d = 60 mm.
examples.answer: Stiffness governs: d ≥ 58.4 mm against 37.0 mm for strength. Use 60 mm; the twist is 0.224°/m and the shear stress only 9.4 MPa.

traps: Checking strength only. A part that is strong enough can still twist or sag too much.
Using Z (or J/r) in the deflection check, or I (or J) in the strength check.
Leaving the twist limit in degrees inside θ = TL/(GJ), which gives radians.
Not rechecking after rounding up. The deflection at 34 mm (2.02 mm) is not the one at 33.47 mm (2.15 mm).
Choosing a higher-strength steel to cure excessive deflection. E and G hardly change between steels.

quiz.q: State the strength and stiffness criteria for a machine part.
quiz.a: Strength: σ<sub>max</sub> ≤ S<sub>yt</sub>/n. Stiffness: δ<sub>max</sub> ≤ δ<sub>allow</sub>, and for shafts θ ≤ θ<sub>allow</sub>.

quiz.q: Write the deflection of a cantilever with an end load and of a simply supported beam with a central load.
Which section properties control bending strength and bending stiffness?
quiz.a: Bending strength: the section modulus Z = I/c. Bending stiffness: the second moment I (with E).

quiz.q: Why can a part pass the strength check but fail the stiffness check?
quiz.a: Stress depends on load and Z, while deflection grows with L³ (bending) or L (twist) and depends on I or J and E. A long, slender part can carry the stress safely and still deflect too far.

quiz.q: A tie 500 mm long of area 100 mm² carries 20 kN; E = 200 GPa. Find its extension.
A simply supported beam has P = 8 kN at the centre, L = 1 m, E = 200 GPa and I = 2 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Find the central deflection.
A cantilever's length is doubled with the same end load. What happens to its deflection and its maximum stress?
quiz.a: Deflection PL³/(3EI) rises 2³ = 8 times; the root moment PL, and so the stress, only doubles.

quiz.q: Only the depth of a rectangular beam is increased. Which check gains more?
quiz.a: Stiffness: I ∝ h³ while Z ∝ h², so the deflection falls faster than the stress.

beyond: In machine tools and robots, stiffness limits set by accuracy and vibration usually decide the structure, and finite element models with optimisation resize the sections until all limits are met. A stiff, light frame also raises the natural frequencies away from the running speeds; critical speeds of shafts are treated with shaft design. Search next for structural optimisation, specific stiffness and machine tool frame design.

figure.caption: The beam of the first worked example: stress and deflection, each divided by its allowed value, plotted against the width. A width is acceptable only where both curves are below 1; the stiffness curve crosses at 30.80 mm and the strength curve later, at 33.47 mm, so strength governs and 34 mm is chosen.

spec.aria: Two falling curves against width from 26 to 40 mm: stress over 120 MPa and deflection over 3 mm. They cross the limit line of 1 at 33.47 mm and 30.80 mm. A dotted line marks the chosen width of 34 mm.
